pending_items.title: Rising prices push families to the brink in Yemen’s Hodeidah
pending_items.content:
Hodeidah, Yemen – Standing beside his rented motorcycle taxi near the Othman market in central Hodeidah, Ahmed Arjash starts each day early in the morning looking for passengers, hoping to earn enough to feed his family of six.

In his late 30s, Arjash also delivers small goods for merchants. By evening, he needs to have made enough money to buy flour, rice and bread, and for the day’s rent on the motorcycle. He falls short.

“Before, I would come home with enough food for my family for the day, and maybe save a little to repair the motorcycle or buy medicine if one of my children fell ill,” he told Al Jazeera. “Now, my daily earnings barely cover the fuel or the rent for the motorcycle. Sometimes I go home empty-handed, or with a small bag of food that does nothing for our hunger.”

Across Hodeidah, where the Red Sea port handles the bulk of commercial and humanitarian imports into Yemen’s Houthi-controlled northwest, families are struggling to afford basic goods as renewed fighting compounds the damage of more than a decade of war.

Fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia intensified in July after four years of relative calm, and the Houthis have since made significant advances in Yemen’s southern Red Sea coast region.

Hodeidah port has come under attack by the Saudi-led coalition, but continues to remain open.

In a market in Hodeidah’s al-Salkhana neighbourhood, Umm Sami, a widow raising four children, sells small household goods and takes occasional domestic work. Rising prices have changed how she shops.

“We buy in very small quantities. Sometimes we buy a little flour or oil that lasts just one day because we cannot afford a whole bag,” she told Al Jazeera. “Even bread has become a burden. My children ask for foods they used to eat easily before the war, and I have to stay silent or distract them by talking about something else.”

Across Houthi-controlled areas, a basket of basic foods cost about 7 percent more in September than in August, its highest price in a year, according to the Yemen Joint Monitoring Report. Food was still available in markets the monitors could reach, but families had less money to spend.

Yemen imports about 90 percent of its food, according to the World Food Programme (WFP).

In Hodeidah’s poorest neighbourhoods, families are skipping meals or going without meat, fish, milk and fruit. Families without clean water at home must buy it at high prices, and deteriorating health facilities leave many unable to afford treatment.

Public sector employees whose salaries have stopped entirely or in part, and families whose fixed incomes have been eroded by inflation, are also in need. In May, the World Bank said Yemen’s economy contracted by 1.5 percent in 2025 and projected a further 0.5 percent contraction in 2026.

Fishing, long a mainstay of Hodeidah’s economy, has become a losing trade for some.

“The cost of going out to sea, fishing equipment and fuel has risen a lot, while sales and people’s purchasing power in the city keep fluctuating,” said Salem, a fisherman in his 30s. “Many families no longer buy fish as they used to. Sometimes a fisherman comes back with barely enough to cover the cost of his trip, if he is lucky.”

Saleh, a construction worker paid by the day, said days can pass without anyone hiring him. “If I work one day, the wage is not enough to cover the family’s needs for several days with prices this high,” he said. “Everything has gone up: food, transport, even the simplest household needs, while income stays the same or shrinks.”

Economic analysts say transport, shipping and fuel costs pass directly to consumers , and that risks to regional shipping have raised insurance and freight costs on imports. Weak demand then shrinks the work available to day labourers.

Fighting earlier this year in Hodeidah governorate’s Hays and al-Khokha districts and elsewhere on the Red Sea coast has forced more families from their homes.

On October 2, the WFP said the fighting had cut off its access to about 350,000 people in parts of Taiz governorate and Hodeidah.

The agency said it had reallocated resources from food distributions scheduled for November to sustain its emergency response, and warned of assistance gaps without new funding. Its monitoring in areas it could reach found 74 percent of households unable to meet their basic food needs.

The WFP suspended its activities in areas under the control of the Houthis in September 2025, after the group detained UN staff members.

For Arjash, the war shows in the dwindling number of passengers who can pay to ride his motorcycle.

“People here walk long distances to save on the fare, and anyone who rides my motorcycle taxi haggles over every rial because their pockets are empty,” he said.

“As you can see, I feel helpless in front of my children when they ask for something simple and I cannot provide it.”

pending_items.title: Why Israel should be afraid of the ICJ genocide ruling against Myanmar
pending_items.content:
There are many reasons why Israel will be deeply worried by the International Court of Justice's finding on 19 November that the military junta in Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority nearly a decade ago.

The president of the world's highest court, Yuji Iwasawa, concluded that Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and tried to hide its crimes through "extensive destruction of evidence".

During so-called " clearance operations " in 2017, Myanmar's security forces from the Buddhist-majority state of Myanmar killed at least 10,000 Rohingya, a Muslim minority, and drove more than 700,000 from their homes in northern Rakhine state. Most found refuge in Bangladesh.

Entire villages were erased, evidence destroyed by burning bodies and bulldozing sites, and the Rohingya subjected to campaigns of rape and sexual violence. Myanmar failed to prosecute the perpetrators.

So what are the implications for another prominent genocide case being considered by the ICJ, this one brought against Israel by South Africa, and backed by more than a dozen other countries, including Ireland, Belgium, Spain and the Netherlands?

Back in January 2024, just weeks into Israel's onslaught in Gaza , the World Court found a "plausible risk" that Palestinians there were being subjected to genocide .

It also imposed a series of provisional measures on Israel to ensure its military did not commit genocidal acts, that aid was allowed in, that all incitement stopped, and that the destruction of evidence was prevented. Israel ignored all of these obligations.

First, the ICJ ruling against Myanmar has set a legal precedent. It is the first time the court has found a state guilty of genocide. It clears a path for the United Nations court to make the same finding, based on even more damning evidence, against Israel.

The bar for establishing genocide has always been higher than for proving war crimes or crimes against humanity because, critically, it requires demonstrating intent by the state under investigation.

In ruling against Myanmar, the court noted that the regime had encouraged anti-Rohingya hate speech, portraying the minority as "sub-human" and posing a "violent threat". This rhetoric, in the view of the judges, exposed the deeper reasoning behind Myanmar's "clearance operations".

In Israel's case, it should be easier to establish intent than it was with Myanmar. Nine pages of South Africa's 84-page submission (59-67) to the ICJ were quotes from Israeli leaders, from the prime minister down, expressing genocidal intent towards Gaza's civilian population.

As is often pointed out, this was the most publicly confessed crime in history.

Israel could carry out operations to eradicate Hamas, or disarm it, and still be committing genocide

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu compared Gaza's Palestinians to Amalek. In the Bible, the Israelites are ordered by God to kill every last Amalek man, woman and child, leaving no one alive. In other words, to commit a genocide.

Former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant called the people of Gaza "human animals" and insisted they be denied all food, water and fuel.

President Isaac Herzog declared no one in Gaza, not even its children, to be innocent: "It is an entire nation out there that is responsible. It is not true this rhetoric about civilians not aware, not involved. It's absolutely not true."

The record of genocidal incitement by Israel's leadership is indisputable.

Second, the ICJ rejected Myanmar's defence that its violence was a justifiable response - that it was counterterrorism - following violent attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army .

The judges ruled that the junta could be pursuing more than one strategy at the same time, and that its military actions to kill rebel fighters could run in parallel to a wider policy of targeting the civilian population.

This is precisely where Israel's narrative is likely to come unstuck.

Israel and its apologists prefer to start the clock with Hamas's one-day breakout on 7 October 2023 from long-besieged Gaza - effectively a concentration camp for Palestinians engineered by Israel over the preceding decades.

Hamas's short, bloody attack inside Israel did not initiate the violence. As the ICJ found in a separate advisory opinion in 2024, Israel has committed crimes systematically against the Palestinian people for decades - and long before October 2023.

That includes an illegal and brutal military occupation , the forced transfer of Palestinians from their homes so Jewish settlers can colonise their land, the prolonged siege of Gaza, and a violent regime of apartheid rule against Palestinians.

More specifically, Israel has claimed its carpet-bombing of Gaza, and its destruction of essential civilian infrastructure - homes, hospitals, schools, government offices, bakeries, agricultural land - is warranted by its efforts to "eradicate Hamas".

In the Myanmar ruling, the ICJ showed it is likely to give short shrift to such rationalisations.

Israel could carry out operations to eradicate Hamas, or disarm it, and still be committing genocide. In fact, it could do so precisely to remove the possibility of resistance to its war crimes and make the task of committing genocide easier.

Third, Myanmar argued that, if its goal was genocide, it could have killed far more Rohingya than it actually did. Estimates are that the junta's actions most likely killed between 1 and 2 percent of the Rohingya people.

The ICJ found, in accordance with the 1948 Genocide Convention, that genocide is not a numbers game. Once intent to destroy a people in whole or part is established, other practices - such as preventing births, forcibly displacing the population, and making their lands uninhabitable - also qualify as genocide.

Israel and its apologists have wilfully sought to mislead about the convention's definition, treating the Holocaust as the only model of what a genocide looks like.

Their argument rests heavily on the false idea that genocide is indeed about numbers, and that Israel would have wiped out everyone in Gaza were it actually bent on genocide.

Netanyahu has regularly articulated this sentiment. In August 2025, for example, he told a press conference: "If we had wanted to commit genocide, it would have taken exactly one afternoon."

Again, the ICJ is unlikely to entertain this as a defence.

Netanyahu's logic intentionally obscures the obvious fact that, in an age of international law, states like Myanmar and Israel have a vested interest in concealing their genocidal intent both by carrying out their crimes incrementally and by offering military rationales as a cover story.

Based on the Rohingya ruling, the number of dead in Gaza is sufficient to qualify as genocidal violence. The known death toll, at nearly 75,000, is more than 3 percent of Gaza's population - and double the percentage of known Rohingya fatalities at the hands of Myanmar's junta.

The Gaza estimates, however, are likely to be a severe undercount, given that many Palestinians were buried under rubble or vaporised by US-supplied 2,000lb bombs. It is also a count of those killed by Israeli weaponry, not those who have died as a result of the dire conditions Israel has engineered in the enclave.

The Israeli military's own assessments are also damning. According to their tally, revealed in August 2025, more than four in five of the dead were civilians, not Palestinian fighters.

Fourth, the ICJ found that Myanmar had committed genocide in three of the convention's five categories: the mass killing; causing serious bodily and mental harm through torture, physical injuries and sexual violence; and preventing births within the group by targeting children and reproductive organs.

Israel has clearly committed crimes on a significant scale in these same three categories, plus it has violated an additional, fourth category of the convention.

As noted earlier, both numerically and proportionally, Israel has killed more Palestinians than Myanmar killed Rohingya. UN bodies have repeatedly found that Israel has caused serious bodily and mental harm to the people of Gaza.

Nearly one in ten Palestinians there are known to have been maimed by Israel's attacks, and nearly everyone has been left with deep mental scars from Israel's relentless bombing campaigns, the equivalent of unleashing at least six Hiroshimas over the tiny enclave.

In addition, thousands of Palestinians - men, women and children - have been seized from Gaza and held in detention camps where torture and sexual violence are reported to be rife. Inmates often emerge severely malnourished .

In June, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel was deliberately targeting children in Gaza. It said these acts "form part of a deliberate strategy to destroy the future of the Palestinians in Gaza by targeting their children".

Independent witnesses, such as international doctors volunteering in Gaza, have testified that soldiers appear to be playing horrifying games in which they compete with each other to show off their prowess as snipers.

Each day, according to the doctors , the soldiers target a different body part: the neck, the abdomen, the testicles.

The ICJ also has plenty of evidence to find against Israel in an additional category in the Genocide Convention, that of creating conditions destructive to life.

In Myanmar's case, the ICJ ruled that evidence the Rohingya had been confined in internment camps where they were denied basic healthcare was not sufficient to meet this fourth category.

In Israel's case, by contrast, Palestinians have not only been denied access to health services. Israel has systematically gone about destroying the entire healthcare system and blocking the entry of medicines and medical equipment.

It has subjected the people of Gaza to sustained starvation, creating widespread malnutrition that scientists warn will cause lasting genetic harm.
